guides.title: Dangote vs BUA Cement in Lokoja: How to Choose
guides.seoTitle: Dangote vs BUA Cement in Lokoja | Buying Guide
guides.description: A practical comparison of Dangote and BUA cement for builders in Lokoja, Kogi State, including strength grades, common uses, storage and what to confirm before buying.
guides.intro: Dangote and BUA are two of the most common cement brands on building sites in Nigeria. Both can produce strong concrete and mortar when the correct grade is used, the mix is right and the cement has been stored properly. The better choice for your project usually comes down to the required strength class, availability, price on the day and how the bags have been handled.

sections.heading: Start with the strength class, not the brand
paragraphs: Cement is supplied in different strength classes, commonly 32.5 and 42.5. The class describes the cement's strength performance, not a guarantee that one brand is always better than another.

For general blockwork, plastering and light concrete, a 32.5 class cement may be suitable. For structural concrete such as columns, beams and suspended slabs, a 42.5 class is often specified. Always follow the specification from your engineer or building professional for structural work.

sections.heading: What Dangote cement is commonly used for
paragraphs: Dangote cement is widely available across Nigeria and is used for blockwork, concrete, plastering and general building work. Its popularity means most contractors are familiar with how it behaves in common mixes.
Availability can vary by location and batch. Confirm the grade you need and check that the bags are intact, dry and within the manufacturer's stated shelf life.

sections.heading: What BUA cement is commonly used for
paragraphs: BUA cement is also used across residential and commercial projects, from foundations and blockwork to plastering and finishing. Many builders choose between the two brands based on the current price and confirmed stock at the depot.

As with any cement, the mix design, water ratio, curing and storage matter more than the logo on the bag. A cheap bag that has absorbed moisture can cost more in wasted work than a well-stored premium bag.

sections.heading: How to check cement before you buy
paragraphs: Check the bag for tears, damp patches, hardened lumps and clear batch or production information. Powder that has partially set is not suitable for structural work.
Ask how the cement has been stored at the depot. Bags should be raised off the floor, kept dry and protected from rain. At your site, use the oldest stock first and keep bags covered.
bullets: Confirm the strength class required for the work.
Check bag weight and packaging condition.
Look for hardened lumps before mixing.
Store on pallets in a dry, ventilated area.
Use cement within the manufacturer's recommended period.

sections.heading: Price, availability and delivery
paragraphs: Cement prices change with supply, fuel costs and market conditions. A quote from last month may not reflect today's price, so confirm the current rate and available quantity before sending a vehicle or making a transfer.
If you are buying in bulk, plan delivery access and offloading before the truck arrives. Cement is heavy and needs dry storage on site.

faqs.question: Is 42.5 cement always better than 32.5?
faqs.answer: Not automatically. The right class depends on the specification and the work being done. Follow your engineer's specification for structural concrete.

faqs.question: How should cement be stored on site?
faqs.answer: Keep bags dry, raised off the floor and covered from rain. Use older stock first and avoid stacking bags against damp walls.

faqs.question: Can I mix cement brands on one project?
faqs.answer: It is generally better to follow the project specification and avoid mixing brands within the same structural pour unless an engineer approves it.

guides.title: Iron Rod Sizes and Uses: 6mm to 12mm Explained
guides.seoTitle: Iron Rod Sizes and Uses in Nigeria | 6mm to 12mm Guide
guides.description: Understand common iron rod sizes used in Nigerian construction, from 6mm stirrups to 12mm and larger reinforcement, and what to check before buying in Lokoja.
guides.intro: Iron rods, also called reinforcement bars or rebar, give concrete the tensile strength it lacks on its own. The correct bar size and spacing depend on the structural design. This guide explains where common sizes are typically used so you can ask better questions and avoid buying the wrong material.

sections.heading: Why bar size matters
paragraphs: A larger bar carries more load, but bigger is not always better. The structural design specifies bar diameter, spacing, anchorage and lap lengths. Using the wrong size can reduce safety or waste money.
For any structural element, follow the drawings and instructions from a qualified engineer or building professional. The notes below are general guidance, not a substitute for a design.

sections.heading: Common sizes and typical uses
paragraphs: Smaller bars are often used for links, stirrups, mesh and light work, while larger bars are used in columns, beams and slabs. Availability and standards can vary, so check the markings and ask for the mill certificate where required.
bullets: 6mm: links, stirrups and light mesh work, subject to design.
8mm: stirrups, mesh and light reinforcement where specified.
10mm: slabs, beams and columns depending on the structural design.
12mm: columns, beams, slabs and other structural elements where specified.
16mm and above: heavier structural work where the design requires it.

sections.heading: What to check before buying iron rods
paragraphs: Look for clear markings, consistent diameter along the length and a reputable supplier. Rust on the surface is common, but deep pitting or excessive scale should be assessed.
Confirm the length of each bar, the unit price and whether the price is per length or per tonne. Keep the receipt so the quantity and grade can be verified later.
bullets: Confirm the diameter and length with a tape or caliper.
Check for bends, cracks or severe corrosion.
Ask for the brand and mill information.
Store rods off the ground and protected from prolonged moisture.

sections.heading: Laps, spacing and bending
paragraphs: Lap lengths, spacing and bend diameters are structural requirements. Do not guess these on site or copy them from a different building. Incorrect laps and bends can seriously weaken the work.
When cutting and bending, follow the bar bending schedule. Keep cut lengths organised and labelled so the fixing team does not mix sizes.

faqs.question: Can I use 10mm rods instead of 12mm?
faqs.answer: Only if the structural design allows it. Substituting bar sizes without engineering approval can reduce the strength of the element.

faqs.question: Should I remove rust before using iron rods?
faqs.answer: Light surface rust is common and usually not a problem, but deep pitting, cracks or severe section loss should be checked by a professional before use.

faqs.question: How are iron rods sold?
faqs.answer: They are often sold per length or by weight. Confirm the unit, length and current price with the supplier before ordering.

guides.title: How to Estimate Cement and Blocks for a Building Project
guides.seoTitle: Cement and Block Estimation Guide for Builders in Nigeria
guides.description: A practical introduction to estimating blocks, mortar and cement for blockwork, with simple examples and important cautions for builders in Lokoja and Kogi State.
guides.intro: Material estimates help you plan purchases and reduce repeated trips to the depot. The exact quantities depend on the block size, wall thickness, mortar mix, openings and workmanship. Use the methods below as a planning guide and confirm the final quantities with your builder or quantity surveyor.

sections.heading: Estimate the wall area first
paragraphs: Measure the length and height of each wall and multiply to get the gross area. Add the areas of all walls, then subtract doors, windows and other openings.
For a simple rectangular room, measure all four walls separately. Irregular buildings should be broken into smaller rectangles and added together.

sections.heading: Convert wall area to blocks
paragraphs: The number of blocks per square metre depends on the actual block size and mortar joint. A common 9-inch block is often estimated at around 10 blocks per square metre, but this varies. Confirm the block size supplied in your area and add a sensible allowance for cutting and breakage.
For planning, divide the net wall area by the coverage of one block, then add an allowance. Always confirm with your builder before ordering a full load.
bullets: Measure net wall area after subtracting openings.
Confirm the actual block dimensions.
Add an allowance for cuts, breakage and future repairs.
Order in stages if storage or site security is limited.

sections.heading: Estimate mortar and cement
paragraphs: Mortar quantity depends on the block type, joint thickness and mix ratio. A richer mix uses more cement; a leaner mix may be suitable for some internal work but must still meet the specification.

Cement is usually sold in 50kg bags. The number of blocks laid per bag varies widely with the mix and workmanship, so use a site-tested figure or your builder's estimate rather than a single internet rule.

sections.heading: Keep a simple material schedule
paragraphs: List each material, unit, estimated quantity and actual quantity purchased. Record deliveries and usage so you can spot waste early.
Buying everything at once can reduce trips, but it also increases storage risk. Cement and other moisture-sensitive materials need dry, secure storage.

faqs.question: How many blocks are in one square metre?
faqs.answer: It depends on the actual block size and mortar joint. A common estimate is around 10 blocks per square metre for a standard 9-inch block, but confirm with the block size and your builder.

faqs.question: How many blocks can one bag of cement lay?
faqs.answer: There is no single figure. It depends on the mortar mix, block size, joint thickness and workmanship. Use a site-tested estimate or your builder's calculation.

faqs.question: How much extra should I buy for breakage?
faqs.answer: A small allowance is sensible for cutting and breakage, but the right percentage depends on the design and handling. Ask your builder to include an allowance in the estimate.

guides.title: Roofing Sheets and Ceiling Materials: Buying Guide
guides.seoTitle: Roofing Sheets and Ceiling Materials Buying Guide | Lokoja
guides.description: What to measure and confirm before buying roofing sheets, ceiling boards and accessories for a building project in Lokoja, Kogi State.
guides.intro: Roofing and ceiling materials are a significant part of the building budget. Buying the wrong profile, gauge or accessory can cause leaks, wasted sheets and delays. Measure carefully, confirm the specification and order the accessories together with the main sheets.

sections.heading: Measure the roof, not just the building
paragraphs: Roof area is larger than the floor plan because of the slope, overhangs and eaves. Measure the length and width of each roof plane, including overhangs, and calculate the area of each plane separately.
For complex roofs, ask your roofing contractor for a roof plan and sheet layout. The layout should show sheet lengths, overlaps, ridges, valleys and flashing.

sections.heading: Confirm the sheet profile and gauge
paragraphs: Roofing sheets come in different profiles, lengths and thicknesses. The required gauge depends on the span, purlin spacing and design. A thinner sheet may be cheaper but can be unsuitable for the span or wind exposure.
Confirm the manufacturer, coating, colour and warranty terms. For long sheets, check transport and lifting arrangements before ordering.

sections.heading: Do not forget the accessories
paragraphs: Ridges, eaves, valleys, flashing, screws, washers and sealants are part of the roof system. Missing or poor-quality accessories are a common cause of leaks.
Order accessories at the same time as the sheets so the profiles and colours match. Use the recommended fasteners and avoid over-tightening screws.
bullets: Ridge caps and matching end caps.
Eaves and barge boards where required.
Valley and flashing pieces for intersections.
Roofing screws with washers.
Sealant and touch-up paint.

sections.heading: Choosing ceiling materials
paragraphs: Ceiling boards are available in different materials and thicknesses, including fibre cement, gypsum and PVC systems. The right choice depends on moisture, fire performance, weight, finish and budget.
For bathrooms, kitchens and exposed areas, consider moisture resistance and ventilation. Confirm the board size, thickness and the matching framing system before buying.

sections.heading: Check quantities and delivery
paragraphs: Add a realistic allowance for cutting, damage and future repairs. Long roofing sheets need careful handling and a clear route to the roof; confirm the delivery vehicle and offloading plan before dispatch.

faqs.question: How do I calculate the number of roofing sheets?
faqs.answer: Calculate the area of each roof plane, divide by the effective coverage of one sheet after overlaps, and add an allowance for cutting and waste. A roofing contractor should confirm the final layout.

faqs.question: Which is better: fibre cement or PVC ceiling?
faqs.answer: It depends on the room, moisture, fire performance, finish and budget. Ask about the product's intended use and installation requirements before choosing.

faqs.question: Should I buy roofing accessories from the same supplier?
faqs.answer: Buying the main sheets and accessories together helps ensure the profiles, colours and fasteners match.

guides.title: Plumbing Materials Checklist for a New Building
guides.seoTitle: Plumbing Materials Checklist for New Buildings | Lokoja
guides.description: A room-by-room checklist of common plumbing pipes, fittings, tanks and tools to plan before starting plumbing work in Lokoja, Kogi State.
guides.intro: A plumbing project runs more smoothly when the main materials are confirmed before work starts. The exact list depends on the building design, water source and number of fixtures. Use this checklist to organise your enquiry, then confirm sizes and quantities with your plumber.

sections.heading: Start with the water source and storage
paragraphs: Confirm whether the building will use mains water, a borehole, a well, a tanker or a combination. Plan the storage tank capacity, pump requirements and overflow arrangement.
Check the space available for tanks and the route for pipes. Confirm whether the tank will be elevated or ground-mounted and what support structure is required.

sections.heading: Pipes and fittings
paragraphs: Pipes are sized according to the fixtures and the length of the run. Your plumber should specify the sizes for the mains, distribution lines, WC connections and drainage.
Use fittings that match the pipe material and pressure rating. Avoid mixing incompatible materials or using damaged fittings.
bullets: Service pipe from the water source.
Distribution pipes for cold and hot water.
Elbows, tees, couplers, reducers and unions.
Valves for isolation and control.
Drainage pipes, traps and inspection points.
Pipe clips, brackets and sealant tape.

sections.heading: Fixtures and sanitary ware
paragraphs: List the fixtures room by room: kitchen sink, bathroom basins, WC, shower, bathtub, washing machine point and outdoor tap. Each fixture needs the correct connection, trap and isolation valve.
Confirm the fixture sizes and any special requirements before roughing in. Changing a fixture late can mean breaking walls or redoing connections.

sections.heading: Testing and handover
paragraphs: Pressure-test the pipework before closing walls or floors. Check for leaks at joints, valves and fixture connections, and confirm that drainage flows freely.
Keep a simple diagram of the pipe routes and isolation valves. Label the main valves so the building can be maintained without guesswork.

faqs.question: What pipe sizes do I need?
faqs.answer: Pipe sizes depend on the fixtures, water pressure and run lengths. Ask your plumber to specify the sizes for your building rather than guessing.

faqs.question: How big should my water tank be?
faqs.answer: Tank size depends on the number of occupants, daily use and how often water is supplied. Your plumber or supplier can help estimate the right capacity.

faqs.question: Should pipes be tested before the walls are closed?
faqs.answer: Yes. Pressure-test the pipework and check for leaks before covering it. Fixing leaks after tiling or plastering is much more expensive.

guides.title: Building Material Delivery in Lokoja: What to Prepare
guides.seoTitle: Building Material Delivery in Lokoja | Preparation Checklist
guides.description: Prepare your site for a building material delivery in Lokoja: access, offloading, quantity checks, payment confirmation and storage.
guides.intro: A smooth delivery depends on more than the truck arriving. Safe access, a clear offloading area and someone ready to count the goods can save hours of delay. Use this checklist before ordering cement, blocks, sand, iron rods, roofing or other materials.

sections.heading: Confirm the order and delivery details
paragraphs: Confirm the product, quantity, unit, price and delivery location in writing. If the order changes, update it before dispatch rather than after the vehicle has loaded.
Check the delivery date and the phone number the driver will call. Make sure the person receiving the goods knows what is coming.
bullets: Full material list with quantities and units.
Delivery address and nearest landmark.
Contact name and phone number.
Preferred delivery date and time window.
Payment and delivery-fee confirmation.

sections.heading: Check site access
paragraphs: Walk the route the truck will use. Check for narrow gates, low cables, soft ground, steep slopes and parked vehicles. A vehicle that cannot reach the offloading point can delay the entire delivery.
Confirm whether the truck can turn around safely after offloading. For long materials such as roofing sheets or iron rods, check the space needed to unload without bending or damaging them.

sections.heading: Prepare the offloading area
paragraphs: Clear the offloading area before the vehicle arrives. Provide firm ground for heavy loads and enough space to stack materials safely.
Have the right number of people available to offload. Cement, blocks and sand are heavy; do not expect the driver to provide labour unless that was agreed.

sections.heading: Check the delivery before offloading
paragraphs: Count the items and compare them with the receipt or invoice. Check the brands, sizes, quantities and visible condition while the vehicle is still at the site.
Report any shortage, damage or incorrect item immediately. Take photos and keep the delivery documents until the issue is resolved.

sections.heading: Store materials correctly
paragraphs: Cement needs a dry, raised and ventilated store. Iron rods should be kept off the ground and away from prolonged moisture. Timber should be stacked flat and protected from rain. Roofing sheets should be handled carefully to avoid scratching and bending.
Plan storage before the delivery. Materials that sit in the rain or in an insecure area can lose value quickly.

faqs.question: Can the driver help with offloading?
faqs.answer: Offloading arrangements depend on the delivery agreement. Confirm before dispatch whether labour is included or whether you need to provide people to offload.

faqs.question: What if the truck cannot reach my site?
faqs.answer: Tell us about narrow roads, soft ground or low cables before dispatch. We may need a smaller vehicle or a different offloading point.

faqs.question: What should I do if materials are missing?
faqs.answer: Count the goods before offloading is completed and report any shortage immediately with your receipt and photos. Do not sign off a delivery you have not checked.
